served.stem: Diethyl 2-methyladipate (shown) is treated with sodium ethoxide and then acid. Of the two possible Dieckmann ring closures, which beta-ketoester is the major product?
served.bankWhy: Dieckmann is reversible and is driven by deprotonation of the product's carbon flanked by both carbonyls. If the methyl-bearing alpha carbon attacks the far carbonyl, that carbon becomes quaternary (option B) with no acidic proton, so that path reverses. The favored product comes from the unsubstituted CH2 enolate attacking, leaving an acidic alpha proton on the ester-bearing ring carbon: option A (C9H14O3), verified to equal the path-B closure.

answer.line: Both rings can close, but only this one keeps an H between the two carbonyls. Ethoxide takes it, and that locks the product in.

steps: Find the two alpha carbons: C2, a CH carrying the methyl, and C5, a CH2. Each can attack the ester at the other end.
Count both rings: each closes five atoms. The C5 enolate leaves a CH between ketone and ester; the C2 enolate leaves a carbon with no H at all.
Dieckmann is reversible until ethoxide pulls that doubly activated H. Only the first product has one. The other ring reopens and everything drains to it.

choices.note: Same formula as the key, but the methyl carbon was counted into the ring. The chain closes five atoms, and the methyl stays outside.
The CH2 end attacks, the methyl rides beside the ketone, and an acidic H sits between the two carbonyls.
This is the product from plain diethyl adipate. Here the 2-methyl group has nowhere to go, so it has to show up in the ring.
This is what a 3-methyl diester would give. Here the methyl sits on an alpha carbon, so it ends up next to a carbonyl, not across the ring.
This ring does form. But its carbon between the carbonyls carries the methyl and no H, so ethoxide cannot lock it in, and it reverts.

student.lockIt: A Dieckmann ends where ethoxide can pull an H from between the two carbonyls.

visual.note: Both closures make five-membered rings. Ethoxide pulling the H between the carbonyls is the step that keeps one.

visual.alt: Diethyl 2-methyladipate, with its CH2 alpha carbon marked as the attacker, gives two possible five-membered rings with NaOEt. The favored ring keeps an acidic H between the ketone and the ester; the other closure puts the methyl there, leaves no H, and reopens.
visual.caption: Look at the carbon between the two C=O groups in each ring. Only one still has an H.
